idiom_name: Grape mounted API with an explicit version strategy + entity/representer DTOs
implementation_notes: Grape turns the pattern's publication step into a framework feature: version 'v1', using: :path (or :header, :accept_version_header, :param) declares the protocol version, one API class per version is mounted on a parent API (newest first) so the surface composes, and the declared params plus entity/representer classes are the contract the consumer sees. The translation layer is the representer or a plain hash builder - ActiveRecord models must never be rendered directly, since to_json publishes every column and turns a schema migration into a wire change. Plain Rack or Sinatra replaces nothing: routing, versioning and documentation all have to be written and maintained by hand, and the protocol drifts as it grows.
code_sketch:
class OrdersV1 < Grape::API
  version 'v1', using: :path
  format :json
  resource :orders do
    params { requires :id, type: String; requires :total, type: Integer }  # contract
    post do
      ack = OrderService.submit(to_domain(params))      # domain stays private
      present ack, with: OrderAckEntity                 # published fields only
    end
  end
end
pitfalls: Rendering ActiveRecord objects directly publishes every column, so a database migration becomes an unintentional wire change.
Grape's params declarations validate input but are not a machine-readable output contract; without a checked-in OpenAPI document (grape-swagger) consumers still guess response shapes.
Reopening or monkey-patching a version's classes makes old versions change under already-integrated clients - a version class must be frozen once published.
